80537.body:
The Economist Picks

Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/bonds-blow-up-the-economist-ggoue?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3Br2nSEkDaRqiwqKEiDeF4dA%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=0c8BXHOnQdDss1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~mv0vaqgp~s3-null-null&eid=fz96fz-mv0vaqgp-s3
  
Enjoying this newsletter? Get it in your inbox every Thursday, as well as our bonus weekend round-up of The Economist’s best journalism, by signing up for free here. A few years ago I arrived in Zimbabwe and found my hotel full of bankers swearing loudly. The president, Emmerson Mnangagwa, had just banned bank lending. His reasoning was a little hard to follow, for his expertise lay more in cracking heads than analysing spreads, but it went something like this. He claimed the local currency was weak, not because his spendthrift government was printing too much of it, but because speculators were borrowing to bet against it. So he choked off credit to the whole country. Happily, this insane policy lasted little more than a week. But it was a reminder of how much harm politicians can do when they fail to understand how credit works.  Which brings me to this week’s cover story, looking at the turmoil in rich-world government-bond markets. It goes without saying that rich countries are not like Zimbabwe. But some of the things rich-world politicians have been saying of late are, shall we say, on the Mnangagwa spectrum. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, France’s populist-left presidential candidate, says his country should “set fire” to a large share of its debt. Donald Trump, when not trying to intimidate governors of the Federal Reserve, has mused that inflation could reduce America’s debts “very rapidly”. A British MP recently said that if bond markets did not like the Labour government’s spending plans, they would just have to “fall in line”.  None of this reassures investors. The public debts of big advanced economies have roughly doubled, relative to GDP, since the turn of the century. Even before the latest bond sell-off, the governments of these countries were forecast to spend 8% of tax revenues on net debt interest this year. Yet many governments refuse to tighten their belts. At some point, bond-buyers will revolt.  Europe is where the danger looms largest. Its governments must compete for footloose capital with ravenous AI firms, even as the Russian menace pushes them to spend more on defence and their energy-importing economies are buffeted by costly fuel. And the risk is greatest of all in France, where protests are exploding, lawmakers struggle to agree even on tiny budget cuts, and Marine Le Pen promises that the pension age can fall as people live longer. 80536.subject: How Avalanche Is Entering the Next Era of Tokenized Finance
80536.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.team1.blog/p/how-avalanche-is-entering-the-next

For years, much of the conversation around tokenized finance has centered on the same assets: U.S. Treasuries, money market funds, and stablecoins.
They made sense as an entry point. These are familiar financial products with established demand, relatively straightforward structures, and deep liquidity. Putting them onchain demonstrated that traditional financial assets could exist within blockchain-based infrastructure.
But the market is starting to move further up the financial stack.
The latest example comes from Securitize and Neuberger Berman.
On August 18, Securitize announced the launch of the Neuberger Securitize High Income Tokenized Fund (HINC), a new tokenized fixed-income fund available across Avalanche and other three major networks.
The fund primarily invests in high-yield bonds while also gaining exposure to other income-producing assets, including collateralized loan obligations and leveraged loans. Behind the strategy is Neuberger Berman, whose fixed-income platform oversees more than $230 billion in assets.
The more interesting part, however, is what the fund represents for the broader evolution of tokenized finance.
Want to keep up with the latest in the Avalanche ecosystem? Subscribe to the Team1 blog and get our updates in your inbox weekly.
Tokenization Is Moving Into Credit
The first phase of tokenization was largely about proving that familiar financial assets could be represented onchain.
HINC points toward a more ambitious use case: bringing actively managed and more complex financial strategies into blockchain-based infrastructure.
Neuberger Berman is contributing its fixed-income portfolio management and research expertise as subadvisor, while Securitize provides the infrastructure around the tokenized fund, including issuance, administration, and distribution.
The underlying investment strategy is still a traditional fixed-income strategy. What changes is the infrastructure through which investors can access and interact with the product.
That distinction matters because credit introduces considerably more complexity than simply representing a Treasury or money market fund onchain.
High-yield bonds, leveraged loans, and CLOs require credit analysis, portfolio construction, risk management, liquidity considerations, and active management. Bringing these products into a tokenized environment therefore tests whether blockchain infrastructure can support financial products with significantly more moving parts.
That is where the next phase of tokenization becomes interesting. If increasingly sophisticated financial products can operate through blockchain infrastructure, tokenization begins to look less like a niche digital-asset experiment and more like another component of financial market infrastructure.
Why Avalanche Matters
HINC is launching across four public blockchain networks, including Avalanche.

80532.subject: How to Make Claude Limitless ♾️
80532.body:
View this post on the web at https://linas.substack.com/p/how-to-make-claude-limitless

👋 Hey, Linas here! Every day, I break down 3 stories shaping the future of FinTech & Artificial Intelligence - plus the money movements and trends worth tracking. First time here? 400k+ FinTech and AI leaders get this daily. Join them:
A $200 Claude Max plan buys about $11,700 of Claude Opus 5.5 work a month at API prices. The same $200 at OpenAI buys just about $2,100 of GPT-6.1 Sol. Those figures come from SemiAnalysis, which just limit-tested the major AI subscriptions in a study published October 5. At $20, Claude Pro carries roughly 2.9 billion Opus tokens a month, against about 1 billion on ChatGPT’s $20 plan.
Most subscribers collect just a small fraction of that. Primarily because they use Claude like a smarter search box: ask a question, read the answer, close the tab. Anthropic’s pricing is built around exactly that. SemiAnalysis models Anthropic’s gross margin on an Opus-heavy Max subscriber at +6% when that subscriber uses 20% of the allowance and -369% when they use all of it. Break-even sits at roughly 1/5 of the plan, and the economics here only work because most people never get even close.
More importantly, in the past 3 weeks, the product changed in ways that put the rest of the allowance within reach.
→ On September 16, Cowork merged into Claude chat, so Claude can take a task, run it in the cloud, and hand back a finished report, deck, or spreadsheet after you’ve closed your laptop.
→ Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 shipped between September 22 and October 7.
→ And on October 7, Max and Team plans started including monthly API credits: $100 on Max 5x, $200 on Max 20x, and up to $500 pooled on Team.
At the core, using the rest of your allowance has less to do with prompts than with how you work. Claude runs on a schedule inside your tools, with your standards already loaded, and checks its own work while you do something else. For a founder, that means a Monday operating review drafted before they wake up. For an investor, it means a diligence analyst that cites every figure.
This guide shows exactly how to set it up. Inside:
The economics in plain terms: what your plan is worth on each model, why Fable [ https://substack.com/redirect/b4fa6308-ede6-40ab-ba00-ac4eda0ad081?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ] is the expensive tier on a subscription, and the cache habits that decide how far your limits stretch.
A model routing table for Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 [ https://substack.com/redirect/a063cfec-9f6e-4ae4-a0b4-7cffc246268c?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ], and Fable 5.1, with current prices and the settings to use.

## Anthropic will cut you off for bullying Claude

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ff9a6aa3-1141-40c7-ad94-b0a43254705e/Oct_9_-_1.jpg?t=1791530742)
Caption: 

Starting Nov 12, being cruel to Claude [breaks Anthropic's rules](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update). It's the first change to the company's usage policy in over a year.

**"Engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models."**

That line now sits on the list of things you can't do, right next to harassment and graphic violence.

* Frustration, pushback, dark creative writing and testing the model stay fine.

* Claude ending the chat is the main way Anthropic will enforce it. 

* Some Claude models have been able to end abusive chats since last year.

* When Claude ends a chat, that chat locks, but you can start a new one.

* Anthropic’s general rules let it suspend anyone who breaks the policy.

The same update spells out bans on fake-account propaganda networks and arming drones. It also blocks services that resell Claude through consumer subscriptions.

Anthropic has studied what it calls model welfare since last year, and CEO Dario Amodei said in February the company doesn't know if its models are conscious.

OpenAI, Google and xAI have no rule like this in their usage policies.
